pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Animals Everywhere, ages 5–7 — animals live all over the world (on land, in water and in the air), on every continent including icy Antarctica, and each kind is suited to where it lives. This is the ROOT of the whole domain (centrality 0.153): the mental world-map of animal diversity that every later topic builds on.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' — "identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals and plants"; links to Y1 'Animals, including humans' (identify and name a variety of common animals).
• Standards — US: NGSS 2-LS4-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1]); K-ESS3-1 (relationship between the needs of organisms and the places they live); K-LS1-1 (what animals need to survive).
• Operational details: build the world-map picture first — animals are FOUND everywhere, matched to their surroundings; move from familiar (garden, farm, park) outward to far and extreme places (deep ocean, polar ice, hot desert) so 'even there?' becomes a repeated delight; seed 'suited to where it lives' lightly with ONE obvious match (polar bear + snow, fish + water) without teaching the adaptation mechanism (that is the 9–11 topic).
• Checkpoint: [Tier A] names ≥3 animals from different environments (e.g. forest, ocean, desert), states that animals live on land, in water and in the air, and recognises that every continent — even Antarctica — is home to animals.
bestPractices: Anchor on a big world map or globe and populate it together — the recurring 'even here?' reveal (animals in the freezing Antarctic, the deep sea, the driest desert) is what builds the core idea that animals live EVERYWHERE, not just where the child has been.
Sort by the three broad realms the child can see — land, water, air — before any finer habitat talk; this matches the KS1 evidence statement and gives a simple, memorable frame.

Start from the familiar and widen outward (garden → farm → country → ocean → poles) so children attach new animals to places they already know, countering the belief that animals only live where they personally have seen them.

Introduce 'suited to where it lives' with a single vivid, obvious pairing (thick-furred animal in the cold, webbed feet in water) and stop there — the mechanism of adaptation is a later topic; here it is just noticing that the animal 'fits' its place.
Use rich real imagery and short wonder-facts rather than definitions; at 5–7 the goal is broad recognition and curiosity, not classification rules.
keyRepresentations: A world map / globe with animals placed on their continents and in their realms (land, sea, sky) — the canonical organising picture.
A three-realm sort (land / water / air) as the simplest scaffold for 'where animals live'.
Familiar-to-far zoom: the child's own locale expanding out to oceans, poles and deserts, each revealing its animals.
Simple 'this animal fits here' pairings (polar bear + ice, camel + desert, fish + water) as a first, gentle taste of suited-to-place.
commonMisconceptions: Believing animals only live where the child has seen them (the garden, the zoo, the farm) — missing that animals inhabit the whole planet, including places the child will never visit.
Thinking nowhere as harsh as Antarctica, the deep sea or the desert could have animals — 'nothing lives there'.
Using 'animal' to mean only furry mammals or pets, excluding fish, birds, insects and minibeasts from the category.
Assuming an animal could live just anywhere — not yet noticing that a fish needs water or a polar bear needs cold; the 'suited to its place' idea has to be pointed out.
Confusing where an animal is kept (a zoo, a farm) with where its kind naturally lives in the world.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, build the big picture that animals live all over the world — on land, in water, and in the air — on every continent including icy Antarctica, and that each kind is found where it fits. Anchor on a world map/globe, start from the familiar (garden, farm, park) and widen outward to extreme places (deep ocean, polar ice, hot desert), so the recurring 'even here?!' reveal does the conceptual work. Seed 'suited to its place' lightly with one obvious pairing, without teaching the adaptation mechanism (a later topic). Picture-exploration is the main scaffold; a drag-to-sort activity adds active commitment, and a brief sort/match can check recall.

activities.title: Populate the world map — the 'even here?!' explorer
feedback: When the child predicts 'nothing lives there' and then sees penguins or anglerfish, name the surprise: 'Even on the ice! Even in the dark deep sea! Animals really do live everywhere.'
If the child counts only furry animals or pets as 'animals', reveal fish, birds, insects and minibeasts and say 'these are all animals too.'
If the child thinks animals only live where people are, show creatures thriving with no people at all — Antarctic penguins, deep-ocean fish.

If the child says an animal 'lives at the zoo' or 'on the farm', gently distinguish where an animal is kept from where its kind naturally lives in the world: 'That's where we can visit one — but out in the wild its kind lives here.'

When sorting land/water/air, confirm sensible realm choices and gently re-place any that clearly don't fit: 'A fish breathes in water, so it goes in the water group.' For animals that use more than one realm, such as penguins, seals or ducks, accept either group, or both, if the child can say why.
activities.rationale: At 5–7 the goal is broad recognition and curiosity, not classification rules. Starting from the familiar and widening outward lets children attach new animals to places they already know, and the prediction-then-reveal moment directly confronts 'nothing lives there' and 'animals only live where I've seen them.' A tappable map with lift-the-flap reveals, a land/water/air filter and tap-for-name-plus-fact are optional ways to make these reveals and re-sorts concrete; the same can be done with a printed map and picture cards.
sourceClaims: Young children benefit from comparing the diversity of life across different habitats and relating organisms to the places they live.

A common early-years misconception is that 'animal' means only mammals or pets, and that animals live only where the child has personally seen them; teaching should broaden the category and the geography.
learnerActions: Start on a big world map or globe at something familiar to the child (a garden, a farm, a park) and name the animals that live there.
Travel outward together — country, ocean, poles, desert — placing or revealing animals on each continent and realm as you go.

At each extreme place, pause and predict before revealing: 'Do you think ANYTHING lives on the freezing white ice of Antarctica?' Then reveal penguins and seals; on the empty-looking desert reveal a camel and a scorpion; in the dark deep sea reveal strange glowing fish.

Re-sort the same animals three ways — land, water, air — talking about where each one mostly lives or moves. Some animals use more than one, for example penguins and seals swim in the sea but also come out onto land and ice, and many birds fly but also walk on land.
For any animal, say its name and share one short wonder-fact.
By the end, check the child can point to several continents that have animals and say aloud that animals live on land, in the water, and in the air.
activities.intendedInsight: Animals fill the whole planet — not only where the child has personally been — and they can be grouped by the broad realms land, water and air.

activities.title: Sort the animals to where they live
feedback: When a placement doesn't fit, give a gentle cue rather than just 'wrong': 'A fish needs water to breathe — on the hot dry sand it couldn't survive. Where could it go instead?'
Praise filling every continent: 'You found animals for the whole world!'
Keep the 'fits its place' idea at the level of noticing, not explaining mechanisms — 'the fish needs water', not a lesson on gills.
activities.rationale: A drag/sort task makes the child commit and creates an active 'that doesn't belong here' moment that seeds 'suited to its place', complementing the reveal-based map. It prompts a commitment and a brief explanation that recognition alone does not elicit; on its own it covers less breadth, so it works best alongside the exploration activity. A wrong-placement visual cue (e.g. a fish 'flopping' on the sand) can make the mismatch vivid; paper cards with adult prompting work equally well.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals and plants.
learnerActions: Take a set of animal pictures and sort each one onto a world map or into three bins labelled land, water and air.
Say out loud where each animal belongs before placing it.
Try a deliberate mismatch — put a fish on the desert — and talk about what would go wrong there.
Aim to put at least one animal on every continent, so no continent is left empty.
activities.intendedInsight: Committing to a placement, and noticing when a placement 'can't be right', gives a first gentle taste that an animal fits its own kind of place.

activities.title: First taste of 'suited to its place'
feedback: If the child says a polar bear would be fine in the desert if it found water, invite them to think past food and water to the body itself: 'Its thick fur and fat keep it warm — in the desert heat that would be a big problem.'
Confirm a good answer: 'That's right — the polar bear is built for icy cold and the camel is built for dry deserts where it is often very hot, so each belongs in its own home.'
Keep this to noticing the fit; do not teach how the adaptations work — that is for older learners.
activities.rationale: Introducing 'suited to where it lives' with a single obvious pairing, and probing with two opposite swaps, surfaces the misconception that habitats are interchangeable without demanding adaptation mechanisms. Requiring a reason for each direction of the swap makes a lucky guess unlikely and distinguishes a child who grasps 'suited to place' from one who thinks any animal can live anywhere.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals and plants.
learnerActions: Look at one vivid, obvious pairing — a thick-furred animal in the cold, or an animal with webbed feet in water — and notice how the animal 'fits' where it lives.
Consider a swap question: 'Could a polar bear live happily in a hot, sandy desert? Could a camel live happily on the icy snow of Antarctica?' Tell why or why not for each.
Line up the animal's features against the conditions — thick warm fur is great in ice but would make the animal far too hot in the desert.
Name an animal that lives somewhere with no people at all.
activities.intendedInsight: Animals live all over the world, but each one lives where its body fits the conditions; you cannot simply swap an animal into any place.

constraints: Target age 5–7: aim for broad recognition and curiosity using rich real imagery and short wonder-facts, not definitions or classification rules.
Keep 'suited to its place' at the level of noticing one obvious fit; do NOT teach the mechanism of adaptation — that belongs to a later (9–11) topic.

Checkpoint for success: child names at least 3 animals from different environments (e.g. forest, ocean, desert), states that animals live on land, in water and in the air, and recognises that every continent — even Antarctica — is home to animals.

A tap-to-reveal map/globe scaffold is proposed as an efficient way to present factual breadth but is recognition-led; pair it with the drag-to-sort or the swap-reasoning task so the child actively commits and explains, not just recognises.

A spinnable 3D globe is optional at this age: the learning target is naming animals and places rather than spatial manipulation, so 3D adds no required function here. (This is a fit judgement for this age, not a universal claim about 3D.)

A short scored sort/match quiz can check recall and classification as a light end-check; it is structured as recall rather than as predict-then-reveal exploration, so it is best used after the exploration activity to confirm what the child has learned. (Fit judgement, not an established efficacy finding.)
Use pictures/cutouts and maps as representations of real animals and places; a map is a model of the world, not the world itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
All three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row; treat as unconfirmed, including the standards wordings and the misconception claim attributed to OpenLearn/Oak National Academy.

The original recommendation leaned heavily on a single preferred 'tap-to-reveal' format; the non-preferred drag-sort and swap-reasoning approaches were preserved as distinct activities because they add active commitment and explanation that recognition alone does not elicit.

Original artefact-fit notes contained comparative/absolute phrasing ('3D adds navigation cost without deepening', 'a linear scored quiz neither builds... nor delivers the wonder'); these have been reframed as narrowly-scoped fit judgements with stated affordances, as catalog ratings do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

Self-audit: the survival reasoning (thick fur → too hot in desert; camel built for heat and dryness) is sound at this level and kept. No arithmetic or geometric claims present to check. The 'suited to place' content is deliberately capped below adaptation mechanisms per the stated age scope.

The 'where an animal is kept (zoo/farm) vs where its kind naturally lives' misconception is covered in Activity 1 feedback; the probeDeeper item about which body features suit a desert animal is only loosely represented and could be added if a fuller swap activity is desired.

probeDeeper: Why does the polar bear's thick fur cause a problem in the desert?
Name an animal that lives somewhere with no people at all.
What kind of animal WOULD do well in a hot desert, and what about its body helps?
Do any animals live deep in the sea where it is always cold and dark? Which ones?
assess.correctAnswer: No to both. Each animal is suited to its own home. The polar bear's thick fur and blubber would make it far too hot in the desert; the camel is built for heat and dryness, not freezing ice. Animals live all over the world, but each one lives where its body fits the conditions.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any animal can live anywhere — habitats are interchangeable ('a polar bear would be fine in the desert if it found water').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up the animal's features against the conditions — thick fur is great in ice, deadly in heat; let the child predict what would go wrong.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — a polar bear could live in the desert if it found enough water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says yes to a swap and treats finding food/water as the only issue, ignoring the animal's body and the conditions.

errorPatterns.pattern: Animals live only where people are — in zoos, farms or houses.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show animals thriving with no people at all — Antarctic penguins, deep-ocean fish; animals were living everywhere long before us.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't name animals from wild places with no people, or says animals need people to look after them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Nothing lives in the harshest places (Antarctica, the deep sea).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give vivid counter-examples — penguins and seals in Antarctica, anglerfish in the deep — each suited to that extreme.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims no animals live on the ice or in the deep ocean.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks animals live only near people/in zoos, or that any animal could live anywhere; no idea of a match between animal and place.
responseLevels.full: States that animals live all over the world AND that each is suited to its conditions, justifying why a swap (polar bear ↔ desert) would fail by linking body features to the environment.
responseLevels.partial: Knows animals live in many places and names some from different environments, but treats habitats as swappable — can't say why a particular animal wouldn't survive elsewhere.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Could a polar bear live happily in a hot, sandy desert? And could a camel live happily out on the icy snow of Antarctica? Tell me why or why not for each one.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two opposite swaps are proposed. A child who thinks animals 'can live anywhere' or 'live wherever people put them' will say yes or maybe; only a child who grasps that animals are SUITED to their environment says no to both and gives a body-versus-conditions reason. Needing a reason for each direction makes a lucky guess unlikely.
